content:
<Rep. Jamie Raskin>: The question H.J. Res. 1 presents is not really about whether nine should suddenly become a magic number of justices for the Supreme Court. It's about whether this Republican-controlled Congress--which has already surrendered congressional war powers, congressional taxing and tariff powers, and congressional spending powers to a president desiring to be a king--should now permanently relinquish another constitutional power that the Framers gave to us in Article I.
The Framers understood that the more a president seeks to expand the powers of the executive branch, the more important it would be for the other branches of government, Congress and the Judiciary, to exercise our own powers to serve as a structural check on an imperious and rapacious executive branch. That's why we have the power of impeachment, the power of oversight, the power of the purse. Alas, over the last year and a half, we've seen this Republican-controlled Congress act in an utterly obsequious and invertebrate fashion before a President who thinks he can go to war without Congress, impose tariffs without Congress, create billion-dollar slush funds without Congress, give himself and his family permanent immunity for crimes and civil wrongs committed without Congress and reduce the Supreme Court and the federal judiciary to the pure instrument of his will.
Placing loyalty to party over loyalty to the Constitution, MAGA House Republicans have repeatedly declined to act in any way to reject the executive branch's outrageous usurpations. In fairness to the Senate Republicans, they have properly reacted with outrage and scorn for the President's attempts to deal himself $1.776 billion to bankroll his private militia and ship-of-fools political operation. But this joint resolution from House Republicans takes us further down the road of institutional capitulation and surrender.
This is not constitutional conservatism but rather one more legislative abdication that strikes at the very architecture of our republic. The Founding Fathers designed Congress to be the ``predominant'' branch, the one representing the people directly and the one most capable of standing as a bulwark against a president grasping for Kingly powers. As the people's Representatives, we are meant to protect the Constitution, not surrender its authority whenever a president likes his particular stacking and packing of power on the Supreme Court and wants to freeze it into place. But that's what the Administration now demands, and our Republican colleagues fall into line like good little foot soldiers, proactively and permanently ceding another one of Congress's powers to presidential will, for no good reason.
Over the course of our nation's history, Congress has repeatedly exercised its authority to change the size, structure, jurisdiction and other aspects of the Court and federal judiciary, and for a variety of reasons. The Judiciary Act of 1789 established the first Supreme Court with six justices--I guess that would have been unlawful and not to the liking of our friends across the aisle. Then in 1801, President John Adams and Congress shrank the size of the Court from six to five, to limit the incoming President Thomas Jefferson's ability to make appointments--I guess that would have been unconstitutional in the view of our colleagues across the aisle, too. When President Jefferson and his Republican Majority came into power, Congress restored the sixth seat.
In 1807, Congress expanded the size of the court to seven seats when it created the 7th Circuit Court of Appeals, and that became the pattern: there should be one justice for each circuit. Again, in 1837, Congress expanded the number of federal circuits to nine and added the corresponding additional two seats to the Supreme Court, bringing the total number to nine. In 1863, Congress briefly added a 10th Circuit during the Civil War, and of course, added a 10th justice to the Supreme Court, giving President Abraham Lincoln another justice to appoint.
In 1866, Congress abolished the 10th Circuit and then reduced the size of the Supreme Court to seven justices. Congress did so to deny President Andrew Johnson the ability to nominate justices who might undermine Reconstruction. Again, in 1869, President Ulysses Grant increased the Court to nine justices with another Judiciary Act, which set the number at nine, matching the number of justices for the number of federal circuits.
So why would we propose a constitutional amendment now, after this history, to tie our own hands--and the hands of every future Congress--for all time?
This Resolution is obviously meant to cement into place a profoundly partisan and lopsided Supreme Court that was successfully stacked and packed by former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell after the deaths of Justice Scalia and Justice Ginsburg. In the former case, when President Barack Obama nominated Merrick Garland to fill the seat, Sen. McConnell did not even allow hearings, much less a vote--a full 11 months before the next election because he said the people should decide. Of course, the people had decided, by electing President Obama to serve as president for a four-year term. In the latter case, Sen. McConnell rushed Amy Coney Barrett's nomination to a vote less than two weeks before the presidential election.
This measure before us today is not actually a serious effort to improve our constitutional system. It is an attempt to pacify the President, yet again, by freezing the illegitimate Court-packing handiwork of the MAGA Senators into place for all time. Our MAGA Republican colleagues are trying to give away another tool that our Constitution deliberately gave to Congress to check the other two branches simply because Donald Trump is now demanding it.
We shouldn't be surprised. It is entirely in keeping with the pattern we have seen since January 20, 2025, where, under MAGA Republican leadership, congressional power is negotiable while the unprecedented expansion of executive power cannot be stopped and is instead celebrated.
Over the last year and a half, President Trump has sued his own government for $10 billion, attempted to extort a nearly $1.8 billion ``settlement'' slush fund--paid for by the American taxpayers--to reward convicted cop beaters, criminals and other MAGA foot soldiers. He's used the Department of Justice to pursue personal grievances, demanding it investigate and prosecute people the President doesn't like. He started an unconstitutional and ruinous war in Iran. He's diverted funding appropriated by Congress to his own personal vanity projects, dismantled federal agencies, accepted unconstitutional lavish gifts from foreign governments, pardoned convicted drug traffickers, and pocketed millions of dollars from ``deals''' he and his family members have made. And the Republican-controlled Congress has done nothing to stop him.
Meanwhile, gas prices have soared, prices across the economy increased, and inflation is on the rise. Americans are worried about the cost of groceries, the cost of housing, and the cost of healthcare. Families across the country are sitting around the kitchen table trying to figure out how to stretch their paycheck just a little further, while the President says he doesn't think about the American people's finances ``at all.'' Instead, he demands that American families foot the bill for his unconstitutional tariffs, his war of choice with Iran, his billion-dollar White House ballroom, and a triumphal arch in his name, while congressional Republicans refuse to stop him, and refuse to stand up for the American people.
This proposed ``constitutional amendment'' is not headed for ratification; everybody knows that. So, I turn back to the question of whether Congress should permanently surrender another one of its constitutional powers. The Framers answered that question well for us, more than two centuries ago, and I stand with them. Congress was designed to check executive power, not to succumb and surrender to it, so I oppose this resolution.
Jamie Raskin,
Ranking Member.
